newsitem.title: BELGIUM: PAINLESS BELGIAN 1997 BUDGET PAVES WAY TO EMU.
newsitem.headline: PAINLESS BELGIAN 1997 BUDGET PAVES WAY TO EMU.

text.p: The Belgian government on Friday reached agreement on a 1997 budget which should pave the way to European economic and monetary union without damaging consumer confidence.
A government source told Reuters on Friday that an 80 billion franc austerity package will cut Belgium's state deficit to 2.9 percent in 1997 from an estimated 3.0 percent in 1996.
"There is a full agreement on the budget. We will reach the 2.9 percent target without hurting the average consumer too much," the source said.
Cabinet aides will hammer out the final details of the package over the weekend, after which a full cabinet session of the centre-left government is set to approve it on Monday.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene will present the full text of the 1997 budget to the Belgian parliament on Tuesday at 1500 local (1300 GMT).
Dehaene has shied away from raising the already record-high taxes on labour income and from a radical reform of the country's general social security system.
On the taxation side, the 1997 budget hits hard at unhealthy habits -- such as smoking, drinking and driving a car.

On the spending side, Dehaene has made a first stab a reforming Belgium's pension system, which -- in light of the rapid ageing of the population -- is a time bomb under the country's already troubled state finances.
Taxes -- mainly indirect -- will rise by 30 billion francs.

Taxes on petrol will be raised by one franc per litre in October and another franc in January. Taxes on beer will rise by one franc per 25-centilitre bottle, on spirits by 12 francs per 75-centilitre bottle, the source said.
The full council of ministers on Friday morning approved the higher excise duties by executive decree. Most will take effect as of October.
The investment world will also have to contribute.
Retail investors will have to pay a 0.3 percent tax on physical delivery of securities by banks and brokerages.
"A small price for anonymity," one analyst said. For tax reasons, many Belgians avoid holding registered securities and prefer holding bearer stocks and bonds in their safes.
The banks would have to pay a 0.06 percent tax on the amount outstanding in savings books accounts, the tax-free regulated savings accounts which are Belgium's most popular savings instrument.
It was not immediately clear how turnover will be defined, but Belgian media estimated the total cost to the Belgian banking sector at five billion francs.
The source also said that 50 billion francs of spending cuts had been decided in the social security sector.
The most visible measure is a gradual increase of women's retirement age to 65 years from 60 over a 13-year period, although this will have little impact on the 1997 budget.
The government has also decided on a two percent tax on all early retirement pensions.

Most other measures in the social security sector are highly technical. They include a reduction of family allowances for teenagers, a reduction in unemployment benefits for older people and some targetted measures in the health sector.
